Chapter Eight: The Backlash to Progress and the Politics of Division
Every time we take a step forward in the fight against racist ideas, there always seems to be a pushback. As the country tried to reckon with the painful legacies of segregation and mass incarceration, a new kind of backlash started to take shape. It wasn’t really new, though—it borrowed old fears and anxieties, but dressed them up in modern politics.
Think about the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. Politicians and media figures started ringing alarm bells, warning that the nation was somehow under attack. You’d hear talk about so-called “reverse racism,” or claims that immigrants were stealing jobs, or that our cities were falling apart. The faces and names might have changed, but the language? It was all too familiar. The message stayed the same: some people belonged, and others just didn’t.
For a lot of folks, these arguments offered a kind of comfort in a world that felt like it was spinning out of control. Imagine a worker, struggling to get by, being told his struggles were because of newcomers—or because others were getting “special help.” Or a voter, worried about the future, hearing that the country’s greatness was being chipped away by people who wouldn’t fit in.
That’s when it really became clear: the politics of division weren’t just about laws or policies—they were about identity. By stirring up fear and resentment, leaders could rally support for actions that actually hurt those with the least power. The old belief that Blackness—or really, any form of difference—was a problem to be fixed, showed up again in debates about welfare, immigration, and national security.
And for the people on the receiving end, the impact was immediate. Picture a family, fleeing violence in their home country, only to arrive and be met with suspicion and hostility. Or a community coming together to demand better schools or safer neighborhoods, and suddenly being accused of asking for too much.
Most people didn’t notice how these arguments were echoes from the past. The words “fairness” and “equality” were used, but somehow, they justified shutting people out and keeping things unequal. It was a cycle: progress, backlash, and then the long, hard work of slowly rebuilding trust.
But even in the middle of all that division, something else was happening. New coalitions began to form. Young people, activists, and allies started reaching across lines, imagining a future where everyone had a place. The struggle wasn’t just about fighting bad policies—it was about challenging the ideas that allowed those policies to exist in the first place.
The politics of division pulled back the curtain on just how deeply racist ideas were woven into American life. The fight for equality wasn’t only about changing laws—it was about rewriting the stories we tell each other, and ourselves, about who truly belongs.
